title: Algorithmic Behaviors Across Regions: A Geolocation Audit of YouTube Search for COVID-19 Misinformation Between the United States and South Africa
screen_reason: Sock-puppet geolocation audit of YouTube search, 30 January to 9 February 2023, from three US and three South African cities, 48 curated COVID-19 misinformation queries under 4 search filters, yielding 23,020 SERPs and 915,440 search results (10,139 unique videos). Videos were labelled by a classifier trained on expert plus crowd annotations against Google's COVID-19 medical misinformation policy. The paper reports that 31.55% of top-10 search results supported COVID-19 misinformation, a share of items returned by the platform, so CONTENT.

estimates.measure_type: % of top-10 YouTube search results that supported COVID-19 misinformation
estimates.denominator: Top-10 search results across the 23,020 SERPs collected by sock-puppet bots in six cities (three US, three South African) for 48 COVID-19 misinformation queries under four search filters over 10 days; the full dataset is 915,440 search results and 10,139 unique videos
estimates.definition: Video classified as supporting COVID-19 misinformation, i.e. promoting a claim contradicting Google's COVID-19 medical misinformation policy (developed with the WHO) and the health policies of the CDC and South African national health authorities
estimates.misinfo_def: "To determine what constitutes misinformation, we based our annotation heuristics on Google’s COVID-19 medical misinformation policy, which has been developed in partnership with the WHO"
estimates.n: Top-10 results across 23,020 SERPs (exact result count for the top-10 subset not stated; the full audit collected 915,440 search results / 10,139 unique videos)
estimates.source_quote: Our audit, conducted in early 2023, uncovered that 31.55% of the top-10 search results contained COVID-19 misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Section 7 Results, 'Misinformation Bias Across Geolocations', p. 941; restated in Section 8 Discussion and in the Conclusion
estimates.ground_truth_detail: A 7-point annotation scheme was developed by the first author with feedback from expert misinformation researchers, grounded in Google/WHO and CDC policy. Ground truth: 3,075 videos annotated (1,087 by the first author as expert, the rest by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers with three annotations per video; 89 disputed videos re-annotated by the author). 62 classifiers trained and evaluated; the selected classifier reached test accuracy, weighted F1 and macro F1 of 0.85, i.e. a stated 15% error rate. The classifier was trained on English videos only and applied only to English videos; non-English videos were annotated manually.
estimates.moderator_quote: Third, we included the 49 search keywords provided by PesaCheck because the keywords were curated by expert fact-checkers to find misinformative videos. Combining the search queries from all three methods, we obtained 137 search queries. Then, we manually removed duplicate queries, combined similar queries, and randomly selected 6 search queries per topic, resulting in a final set of 48 search queries
estimates.notes: The queries were deliberately curated by fact-checkers to surface misinformative videos, so this figure is an upper bound on what an ordinary COVID-19 searcher would meet: sampling_frame=curated_seed and denom_selection=curated (top-10, rank-truncated) both flag that. Pooled across the two countries; the paper reports country differences only as misinformation bias scores and significance tests, never as separate percentages, so no per-country rows are possible.

missed_or_uncertain: No per-country, per-geolocation, per-topic or per-filter percentage is reported. All of those comparisons (SA > US for top-10 and top-20; US > SA for top-40 and top-50; Houston > Los Angeles; SA > US for '5G Claims', 'Bill Gates Claims' and 'Vaccine Content Claims'; US > SA for 'Spread of Virus') are expressed as misinformation bias scores on a -1 to +1 scale with Mann-Whitney U tests and effect sizes, not as shares of results, so no rows could be made. The topic-level heatmap values (0.45, 0.44, 0.28, 0.29, -0.46, -0.42, 0.01, 0.02, -0.65, -0.67, 0.16, 0.15, 0.17, -0.3, -0.26) are bias scores, not percentages, and the text file does not carry the row labels needed to match them to topics reliably. The complements 36.03% opposing and 32.42% other classes are stated verbatim and recorded in value_raw but are not misinformation shares. The 15% classifier error rate is a material caveat on the 31.55%; the authors report robustness checks for it in Appendix K, which is not in this text file.

rob.design: Sock-puppet algorithm audit, 30 January - 9 February 2023. Six geolocations (Los Angeles, Houston, Jacksonville; Johannesburg, Durban, Cape Town), chosen as the largest city in heavily affected states/provinces, reached through IPRoyal proxies after three validation experiments confirming YouTube personalises on IP geolocation and that the proxies delivered the intended locations. 48 search queries across 8 globally persistent COVID-19 misinformation topics identified with PesaCheck (an IFCN-affiliated African fact-checking organisation), built from three sources including 49 PesaCheck keywords and KeyBERT-extracted keywords, then deduplicated to 6 per topic. Four search filters (including 'Rating'). Output: 23,020 SERPs, 915,440 search results, 10,139 unique videos; one bot in Durban crashed on one day. Labelling: 7-point annotation scheme grounded in Google/WHO and CDC/SA policy; 3,075 ground-truth annotations (1,087 expert, rest AMT with 3 per video and agreement checks); best of 62 classifiers achieved 0.85 accuracy / 0.85 macro and weighted F1. Non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis with Conover-Iman post-hoc and Bonferroni adjustment). Limitations acknowledged by the authors: bots do not have real user histories, so this measures algorithmic supply rather than actual user exposure, and the classifier carries a 15% error rate.
rob.item6_quote: To determine what constitutes misinformation, we based our annotation heuristics on Google’s COVID-19 medical misinformation policy, which has been developed in partnership with the WHO (Google 2020). We also referenced the policies of national health authorities in the US and SA, such as the Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
rob.item10_quote: However, we observe that nearly a third of the top-10 search results were misinformative: 31.55% of the search results supported COVID-19 misinformation, 36.03% were opposing, and 32.42% belonged to the remaining classes.
